beats.say: A man stood in front of the Buddha and insulted him for a long time. Shouting, spitting, calling him every bad name he knew. The Buddha only listened.
When the man ran out of breath, the Buddha asked: If you bring someone a gift, and he does not accept it, whose is the gift? Mine, of course, said the man.
Then I do not accept your anger, said the Buddha. Please, take it home with you.
Osho taught: watch, don't react. An insult is a parcel. You don't have to open it. Let it stay with the one who brought it.
A mother whose little boy had died carried him to the Buddha, begging: Bring my son back to life. Yes, said the Buddha. Bring me one mustard seed.
But it must come from a house where nobody has ever died. She ran from door to door. Everyone had seeds. Nobody had a house without death.
By evening she sat down, empty-handed. And she understood. Death comes to every house. Her grief was not hers alone.
Osho taught: death is not the enemy of life. When loss comes, you are joining everyone who ever loved. Breathe. Let the tears come. Then let them go.
A frog lived at the bottom of an old well. He was very proud of it. This is the greatest place in the world, he told every visitor.
One day a turtle from the great sea looked in, and told him about the ocean. A thousand miles wide, and so deep that nobody has found the bottom.
The frog laughed. Impossible, he said. Nothing can be bigger than my well. And he went back to his little patch of mud.
Osho taught: knowledge is not knowing. Every opinion you hold is a well. Comfortable, small, very sure. Today, climb to the edge, and look at the sky.
A traveller saw a huge elephant tied to a small stick with a thin rope. It could have broken free with one step. But it never even tried.
Why? he asked the keeper. When it was a baby, said the keeper, we tied it with this same rope. It pulled and pulled, but it could not break it. So it stopped trying.
Now it is grown, strong enough to pull down a house. But it still believes the rope is stronger.
What thin rope is still holding you? Osho called it conditioning. I can't. I'm not the type. Take one step today. It will snap.

title: The Eagle Who Lived as a Chicken

beats.say: A farmer found an eagle's egg and put it under one of his hens. The little eagle grew up among the chickens, scratching in the dirt for worms.
One day he saw a great bird gliding high above him, without moving its wings. What is that? he asked. That is the eagle, said the chickens. Don't even dream of it.
So he lived and died as a chicken. Because that is what he thought he was.
You are not what they told you you were. Osho taught: drop the conditioning, and be yourself. You have wings. The sky is waiting.

title: The Stonecutter
ref: A Japanese folk tale · Osho, The Book of Wisdom

beats.say: A poor stonecutter saw a rich merchant pass by, and wished: if only I were rich. And it happened. Then he saw a prince, and wished to be the prince.
As the prince, he wished to be the sun. As the sun, the cloud that covered it. As the cloud, the wind that blew it away.
But the wind could not move the mountain. So he became the mountain. And then he felt someone chipping at his feet. A stonecutter.
Osho said: "Be — don't try to become." Ambition only brings you back where you started, more tired. What if you are enough, right now?

title: The Bird in the Golden Cage

beats.say: A rich man kept the most beautiful bird in the land, in a cage of pure gold. He gave it the best seeds and the cleanest water. And it stopped singing.
A wandering Sufi passed by and asked him: Tell me, do you love the bird... or do you love the cage?
The man stood a long time in silence. Then, with trembling hands, he opened the little door. And the bird flew away into the sky.
The next morning there was singing at his window. Osho taught: love gives roots, and freedom gives wings. Open one door today.

title: The Drop and the Ocean
ref: A Sufi image · Osho, Come, Come, Yet Again Come

beats.say: A raindrop falling from a cloud saw the ocean below, and it was terrified. If I fall in there, it said, I will be lost. I will disappear.
And it was true. It would lose its little shape, its little edge. The drop would be gone.
But the Sufis say: the drop does not die in the ocean. It becomes the ocean. It loses something small, and gains everything.
Osho said: "My whole teaching consists of two words, meditation and love." Not losing yourself, but finding how big you really are. Let one breath fall into the ocean.
A rich man came home and saw his house on fire. Inside, his children were playing, too busy with their toys to notice the flames.
He shouted: Come out, the house is burning! But they did not understand fire. They did not even look up.
So he shouted: Come quickly, I have brought you new toys! And they came running out, and they were saved.
The Buddha said: the world of worry and greed is the burning house. Osho taught the same: wake up, step outside. What waits there is better than any toy.
A man walking home in the dark saw a snake on the path. His heart stopped. He could not move. Sweat poured down his face.
Then a neighbour came by with a lantern. In the light the man saw it clearly. It was only a rope. An old rope, lying in the dust.
Where did the snake go? Nowhere. It was never there. Only the darkness made it.
Osho taught: don't fight the darkness, bring light. Most of your fears are ropes in the dark. Look at the fear, and watch it become a rope.
A water carrier had two pots hanging from a pole. One was perfect. The other had a crack, and every day it arrived at the house half empty.
The cracked pot was ashamed. I am sorry, it said. Because of me, half your work is wasted. Throw me away.
Look at the path, said the water carrier. On your side, all the way from the river, wild flowers were growing. I planted seeds there. You have been watering them.
Osho taught: accept yourself totally. Your cracks are not your failure. Something beautiful is growing through them. Stop hiding them today.

title: The Man Who Carried His Raft

beats.say: A man came to a wide river with no bridge. He tied branches and reeds into a raft, and floated safely to the far bank.
Then he thought: this raft has been so useful. I will never leave it. And he carried it on his head for the rest of his life.
The Buddha laughed. My teachings are like that raft, he said. Use them to get over the river. Then put them down, and walk on.
Osho taught: use a method, then drop it. What are you still carrying that has already done its work? Put it down on the bank.
The Sufi dervishes turn. Round and round, one hand raised to the sky, one hand turned to the earth, for hours.
Their white skirts fly. The room becomes a blur. And yet, if you look at their faces, they are completely calm.
Like a wheel, they say. The rim spins fast. The centre does not move at all. We have found the centre.
Osho made a meditation of this Sufi whirling. You don't have to stop the wheel. Find the still point in the belly, and let everything turn around it.
Three monks travelled through old China. They never preached. They stood in the market square and laughed. Belly laughs, until the whole village laughed with them.
When one of them died, the people thought: now they will weep. But the other two danced around the body, laughing louder than ever.
And when the body was placed on the fire, it burst into fireworks. The dead monk had hidden them in his clothes, for one last joke.
Even his death became a celebration. Osho loved this story: life is too short to be so serious. Laugh once today, for no reason at all.
A poor man stood outside an inn, smelling the soup and eating his dry bread. The innkeeper grabbed him. You smelled my soup. Now pay for it!
They went to the judge, who was Mulla Nasruddin. Nasruddin took some coins from his own pocket, and shook them next to the innkeeper's ear.
Did you hear that? said Nasruddin. Yes, said the innkeeper. Good, said Nasruddin. The smell of your soup is paid for with the sound of my money.
We laugh. Osho loved Nasruddin for that. But how often do we demand payment for what costs nothing? Today, let something be free.
Mulla Nasruddin went to a wedding feast in his old working clothes. Nobody looked at him. Nobody offered him a seat.
So he went home, put on his finest coat with gold buttons, and came back. At once he was welcomed, and seated at the head of the table.
Then Nasruddin took the soup and began pouring it into his pockets. Eat, my coat, eat! he said. It is you they invited, not me.
Osho loved Mulla Nasruddin. Look how much of the world bows to the coat. Don't confuse the coat with yourself. Under it, you are the same.
A proud scholar was taking a ferry over a wide river. He asked the boatman: Have you studied grammar? No, said the boatman. Then half your life is wasted.
The boatman said nothing. In the middle of the river a storm came up, and the boat began to sink.
The boatman asked: Have you learned to swim, sir? No, said the scholar. Then, said the boatman, your whole life is wasted.
Osho taught: knowing about the water is not swimming. Experience, don't believe. Put down one idea today, and take one real breath.
Mulla Nasruddin was the judge of his village. A man came and told his side of a quarrel. Nasruddin listened carefully, and said: You are right.
Then the other man told his side. Nasruddin listened carefully, and said: You are right.
His wife was listening from the kitchen. They can't both be right! she said. Nasruddin thought for a moment, and said: You are also right.
Osho loved Nasruddin's jokes. Truth is bigger than any one side. Before your next argument, take one breath, and see what the other person sees.
One night Mulla Nasruddin looked into his well, and saw the moon lying at the bottom. Oh no, he cried. The moon has fallen in! I must save it.
He tied a hook to a rope and let it down. The hook caught on a stone. He pulled with all his strength... the rope broke, and he fell flat on his back.
Lying there, he saw the moon shining in the sky. Thank God, he said. It was hard work, but I have put it back where it belongs.
Osho taught: the mind lives with reflections. Look up from the well. The real moon is already shining.

title: The Blind Men and the Elephant

beats.say: Some blind men touched an elephant, each a different part. It is a snake, said the one at the trunk. No, a pillar, said the one at the leg.
It is a fan, said the one at the ear. A wall, said the one at the side. A rope, said the one at the tail. And they began to fight.
A wise man passing by said: You are all right, and you are all wrong. Each of you is holding a small piece of something very big.
Osho taught: every belief is one blind hand on the elephant. Hold your piece gently. Today, listen to someone else's.
An old holy man saw a scorpion drowning in the river. He reached into the water and lifted it out. And the scorpion stung him.
It fell back in. Again he lifted it out, and again it stung him. A man watching shouted: Why do you keep saving it? It will only sting you!
The old man smiled through the pain. It is the nature of the scorpion to sting. It is my nature to save. Why should I give up mine because of his?
Osho taught: be yourself, whatever others do. Don't let anyone's poison change who you are. Be kind today.
A young man came to an old teacher, full of bitterness about his life. The teacher said: Put a handful of salt in a glass of water, and drink it.
The man drank, and spat. Terrible! he said. Now, said the teacher, put the same handful of salt into the lake, and drink from the lake.
He drank. It was fresh and sweet. The pain of life is like salt, said the teacher. The amount is the same. What changes is the size of the container.
Osho taught: don't fight pain, become bigger than it. Become a lake, not a glass. Feel how wide you can be.
One day the Buddha sat down before his monks to give a teaching. Hundreds were waiting. But he said nothing. He only held up a single flower.
Minutes passed. The monks were confused. They looked at each other, wondering what it meant.
Only one old monk looked at the flower... and smiled. And the Buddha said: What can be said, I have said. What cannot be said, I have given to him.
Osho loved this story: Zen began with a flower and a smile. Some things cannot be explained. Look at one flower today, without a single word.
In the forest lived a terrible bandit who had killed many people. Travellers took long roads around it. But the Buddha walked straight in.
The bandit ran after him with a sword, screaming: Stop! But however fast he ran, he could not catch the Buddha, who was walking slowly.
Exhausted, the bandit shouted: Stop, monk! And the Buddha turned and said: I have stopped. It is you who has not stopped.
The bandit dropped his sword and wept. Osho taught: life is only here and now. What is still running in you? Stop, for one breath.
A monk kept asking the Buddha great questions. Is the world eternal? What happens after death? Is there a soul? And the Buddha told him a story.
A man is shot with a poisoned arrow. The doctor comes to pull it out. But the man says: Wait! First tell me who shot it, his name, his family, what wood the bow is made of.
While he asks his questions, the poison is spreading. He dies with the arrow still in him.
Osho taught: don't philosophise, experience. Your suffering is the arrow. Pull it out now. Breathe, and look at what hurts.
A young prince became a monk, and he was so hard on himself. No food, no sleep, walking all day until his feet bled.
The Buddha asked him: You used to play the lute. If the strings are too loose, what happens? There is no music, said the monk. And if they are too tight? They break.
And when are they just right? When they are neither too tight nor too loose. Then the music comes.
Osho taught the middle way of the lute: not too tight, not too loose. Where are you pulling too hard today? Loosen one string.
A king asked for a ring that would help him in every situation. An old Sufi gave him a plain one. On it, four words: This too shall pass.
Years later the king lost everything in a war, and hid in a cave, ready to die. He looked at the ring. And he found the strength to go on.
When he won his kingdom back and the whole city was dancing, he looked at the ring again. This too shall pass. And he became quiet.
Osho taught: only the witness remains. Pain passes. Pleasure passes. Whatever you feel right now... this too shall pass.

title: The Bowl That Was Never Full

beats.say: A beggar came to a king's palace. The king said: I will fill your bowl with anything you like. Gold, said the beggar.
The servants poured in gold coins, and they vanished. More gold, and more. The whole treasury went into that little bowl, and still it was empty.
The king fell at the beggar's feet. What is this bowl? It is made from a human skull, said the beggar. It is the human mind. Nothing is ever enough for it.
Osho taught: desire can never be filled, only seen through. Notice the next little voice that says: more. And smile at it.
On a freezing winter night, a wandering monk stopped at a temple. There was no firewood. So he took the wooden Buddha from the altar, and burned it.
The temple priest woke up and screamed: You have burned the Buddha! The monk began poking in the ashes with a stick. I am looking for the holy relics, he said.
Relics? In a piece of wood? shouted the priest. Then why are you angry? said the monk. Bring me the other two. I am still cold.
Osho taught: don't worship the statue, become the Buddha. The real one is sitting where you are sitting.
A man fled from a tiger and jumped over a cliff, catching hold of a wild vine. Above him, the tiger waited. Below him, far down, another tiger.
Then two mice, one white and one black, began to nibble at the vine. Slowly, slowly, it grew thinner.
And beside him, growing out of the rock, he saw one ripe wild strawberry. Holding on with one hand, he picked it with the other. How sweet it tasted!
Osho taught: this moment is the only one there is. Past above, future below. And this moment, sweet in your hand. Taste it.
In Baghdad a servant came running home from the market, shaking. Master, I saw Death there, and she made a sign at me! Lend me your horse. I will ride to Samarra tonight.
The master gave him the horse. Then he went to the market himself, found Death in the crowd, and asked: Why did you frighten my servant?
I did not mean to, said Death. I was only surprised to see him in Baghdad. You see, I have an appointment with him tonight, in Samarra.
Osho taught: don't run from fear, look at it. Running only brings you to it faster. Most fears are shadows.

title: The Parrot Who Played Dead
ref: A Sufi tale (Rumi) · Osho, The Art of Dying

beats.say: A merchant was leaving for India. What shall I tell your cousins there? he asked his caged parrot. Tell them I am in a cage, it said.
In India, when he told the wild parrots, one of them shook, fell from its branch, and lay still. Sadly, he came home and told his own parrot.
At once it fell down in the cage, as if dead. Weeping, the merchant opened the door and laid it outside. And it flew up onto the roof.
My cousin taught me, it sang: die to what holds you, and you are free. Osho said the same: "Let there be a let-go."
A poor man visited a rich friend, drank too much, and fell asleep. Before leaving early the next morning, the friend sewed a priceless jewel into the lining of his coat.
The poor man woke and wandered for years, begging, hungry, never knowing. Every night he slept in the cold with a fortune sewn against his heart.
One day he met his old friend again. Why are you still a beggar? said the friend. Look in your coat. And there it was.
Osho taught: what you are begging for, you already are. Put your hand on your heart now. Feel it.

title: The Man Who Ran from His Shadow

beats.say: There was a man who hated his own shadow, and his own footprints. So he decided to run away from them.
But the faster he ran, the more footprints he left, and his shadow kept up with him easily. So he ran faster, and faster, and faster.
He ran until he dropped dead. He never thought of sitting down in the shade of a tree. In the shade, there is no shadow. Sitting still, there are no footprints.
Osho loved Chuang Tzu. Whatever you keep running from runs with you. Sit down in the shade. Be still, and watch it disappear.
A doll made of salt travelled a long way, until it came to the edge of the sea. It had never seen anything like it. What are you? it asked.
Come in and see, said the sea. So the salt doll stepped into the waves. And as it went deeper, it began to dissolve.
Up to its knees... its waist... its heart. And as the last little piece of salt melted away, it whispered: Now I know what I am.
Osho taught: you cannot know the ocean from the outside. Someday you will have to step in. Take one step tonight, into silence.
A poor woodcutter met a wandering saint in the forest. Go further in, said the saint. So he went further, found a grove of sandalwood, and became rich.
But he remembered: go further. So he went deeper, and found a silver mine. Then deeper still, and found gold. Then diamonds.
And then, deeper than anyone had gone, he found the saint himself, sitting under a tree in complete silence. And he forgot all about the diamonds.
Osho taught: never settle on the way. Whatever you find inside, go further. Close your eyes, and go one step deeper.
Mulla Nasruddin was sitting on the bank of a wide river. A traveller on the far bank cupped his hands and shouted: How do I get to the other side?
Nasruddin looked up the river, and down the river, and thought for a long time.
Then he shouted back: You are on the other side!
Osho loved Nasruddin. We all want to get to the other side. To peace, to freedom, to God. But wherever you stand, you are already there.
Mulla Nasruddin borrowed a big cooking pot from his neighbour. When he gave it back, there was a small pot inside. Your pot gave birth, he said.
A week later Nasruddin borrowed the pot again, and did not return it. When the neighbour came asking, Nasruddin said sadly: I am sorry. Your pot has died.
Died? shouted the neighbour. How can a pot die? Strange, said Nasruddin. You believed it could give birth.
Osho loved Nasruddin's jokes. We believe whatever pleases us, and fight whatever does not. Watch how your mind chooses what is true.
Some moths wanted to know the truth about the flame. The first flew near a candle, came back, and said: It is bright.
The second flew closer, burned its wings a little, and said: It is hot. The wise old moth said: Neither of you knows anything.
Then the third moth flew straight into the flame, and became one with it. Only he knows, said the old moth. And he cannot come back to tell us.
Osho taught: love is not admiring the light from a distance. It is falling into it. What would you fall into, if you were not afraid?
A man spent twenty years practising in the forest, until he could walk on water. Proudly he went to his master. Look what I have learned!
And he walked over the river in front of him. The master watched, and said: Twenty years? The ferryman takes people over for one small coin.
You have spent twenty years of your life, said the master, to learn something worth one coin.
Osho taught: don't chase spiritual tricks. The real miracle is to be fully here. That costs nothing, and you can do it now.
A young boy begged the master for a koan, a riddle for meditation. The master said: You know the sound of two hands clapping. What is the sound of one hand?
The boy went away and listened. He heard music from the town. That is it! he said. No, said the master.
He heard dripping water, the wind, an owl, the crickets. No, no, no. For a whole year he listened, and the master said no to everything.
At last he heard the sound that has no sound. Osho called it no-mind. Listen to the silence itself. One minute, now.
Chuang Tzu and his friend Hui Tzu were walking on a bridge over a river. Look at the fish, said Chuang Tzu. How happy they are, swimming about.
You are not a fish, said Hui Tzu. How can you know what makes a fish happy? You are not me, said Chuang Tzu. How can you know what I know?
They argued back and forth. At last Chuang Tzu laughed. I know it the way I know it, he said. By standing here, on the bridge.
Osho taught: some things are known only by being there. Stand by some water today, and simply know.
Chuang Tzu was fishing by the river when two officials arrived from the king. The king wants you to be his prime minister, they said.
Chuang Tzu kept fishing. I hear, he said, that the king has a sacred tortoise, dead three thousand years, kept in a golden box in the temple.
Would that tortoise rather be dead and honoured in a box, or alive, dragging its tail in the mud? Alive in the mud, they said. Then go away, said Chuang Tzu.
Osho taught: freedom is worth more than fame. Fame is a golden box. Freedom is the mud. Which are you choosing today?
When Chuang Tzu's wife died, his friend came to comfort him, and found him sitting on the floor, drumming on a pot and singing.
How can you sing? said the friend. She shared your whole life! At first I grieved, said Chuang Tzu. Then I saw that before her birth there was no body, no breath.
Out of the great mystery came breath, and a body, and life. Now it has changed again, like spring into summer, summer into autumn. She is resting.
Osho taught: death is part of the dance. Grief is natural. But behind it, see the great turning of the seasons. Breathe with it tonight.
A king gave his best fighting rooster to a trainer. After ten days he asked: Is it ready? Not yet, said the trainer. It is proud and angry.
Ten more days. Not yet. It still flares up at the sight of other roosters. Ten more days. Not yet. It still has fire in its eyes.
After forty days the trainer said: Now it is ready. Other roosters crow, and it does not even move. It stands like a rooster carved from wood.
The other roosters took one look and ran. Osho taught: real strength is silence, not noise. Be a little wooden today.
Confucius was watching a great waterfall, where no fish could swim, when he saw an old man fall into the foaming water.
He sent his students running to save him. But a little further down, the old man climbed out, and walked along the bank, singing.
How do you do it? asked Confucius. I have no method, said the old man. I go down with the swirl, and come up with the swirl. I follow the water, not myself.
Osho taught: let go, and flow with life. Go down with the current. Come up with it. Let it carry you.

title: The Bell Stand
ref: Chuang Tzu · Osho, Hyakujo: The Everest of Zen

beats.say: A master carpenter carved a bell stand so beautiful that people said it must be the work of spirits. How did you do it? asked the prince.
Before I begin, said the carpenter, I fast for three days, and forget about money. Five days, and forget about praise. Seven days, and forget I have a body.
Then I go into the forest and look at the trees, until I see the bell stand already living in one of them. Then I simply set it free.
Osho said: "Your every act should be a ceremony." Forget the reward. Do one small thing today, just for its own sake.

title: The Thief and the Open Drawer

beats.say: A thief with a sword broke in while the old master was chanting. Your money or your life! The master did not even turn. The money is in that drawer, he said.
Leave me a little for the taxes, said the master. And as the thief was leaving: You should thank a person when you receive a gift. So the thief bowed.
Later the thief was caught. But the master told the judge: This man is no thief. I gave him the money, and he thanked me for it.
Years later, the thief came back as his student. Osho taught: share, and grow richer. Give one thing away.
A young teacher came to visit the old master. It was raining, so he left his wooden shoes and his umbrella outside the door.
After greeting him, the master asked: Did you leave your umbrella on the left side of your shoes, or on the right?
The young man could not remember. And he understood that he was not yet awake. He stayed, and studied with the master for six more years.
Osho taught: awareness is not only for the cushion. It is for every minute. Where did you put your keys today? Notice the next small thing you do.
A rich merchant brought five hundred pieces of gold to a Zen master for his new temple. Here, he said. This is a great deal of money.
Very well, said the master, and put it aside. The merchant was annoyed. Five hundred pieces is a lot of gold! Don't you have anything to say?
Why should I thank you? said the master. You should thank me. The giver should be thankful.
Osho taught: give freely, and be glad someone received it. A gift with a hook is not a gift.
Four monks agreed to sit for seven days in complete silence. On the very first night, the oil lamp began to flicker.
The first monk said: Somebody fix the lamp! The second said: We are not supposed to talk!
The third said: Why are you both talking? And the fourth laughed: Ha! I am the only one who has not said a word!
Osho taught: silence is not a shut mouth. It is a quiet mind. Watch how quickly yours wants to speak.
A priest boasted to the Zen master Bankei: My teacher could write a holy name in the air, across a river! What miracles can you do?
Bankei smiled. Perhaps your teacher could do that trick. But that is not the way of Zen.
My miracle is this. When I am hungry, I eat. When I am thirsty, I drink. When I am tired, I sleep.
It sounds so simple. But try it. Osho called this totality. When you eat today, only eat. That is the real miracle.
A duke was reading in his hall when the old wheelwright working outside asked: What are you reading, my lord? The words of the sages, said the duke.
Are the sages alive? No, they are dead. Then you are reading the dregs they left behind, said the old man.
I have made wheels for seventy years, he said. I cannot even teach my son the feel of it. It is in the hands. The sages took theirs with them.
Osho taught: books point, only experience knows. Close the book for a moment, and taste it yourself.
A monkey keeper told his monkeys: You will get three chestnuts in the morning, and four in the evening. The monkeys screamed with rage.
All right, said the keeper. Four in the morning, and three in the evening. And the monkeys were delighted.
The same seven chestnuts. Nothing had changed but the words. And yet the monkeys were happy.
Osho loved Chuang Tzu's humour. How many quarrels are over three in the morning? Let the other side have the words. Keep your peace.
A monk asked the old master Joshu: What is the meaning of Zen? Why did the great teachers come from the West?
Joshu pointed out of the window and said: The cypress tree in the courtyard.
The monk was puzzled. Master, don't answer with things. I am not answering with things, said Joshu. Then what is Zen? The cypress tree in the courtyard.
Osho taught: truth is not far away. It is here, in front of you. Look at one tree today, completely.
There was a monk so slow that he could not learn a single line of the teachings. Even his own brother told him to go home.
The Buddha found him crying, gave him a clean white cloth, and said: Sit in the sun, rub this cloth, and say: removing dirt, removing dirt.
As he rubbed, the white cloth slowly turned grey with the dirt of his hands. And watching it, he suddenly saw: the mind gathers dust in just the same way.
Osho taught: you don't need to be clever. You need one simple practice, done with your whole heart. What is yours today?
When the Buddha came to the city, the king lit ten thousand lamps along the road. A poor old woman had one coin, and bought oil for one small lamp.
In the night a great wind came. One by one, all the king's lamps went out. Only the old woman's little lamp kept burning.
The monks tried to blow it out. They could not. The Buddha said: Leave it. It was lit with the whole heart. No wind can put it out.
Osho taught: it is the heart behind the gift, not its size. Light one small lamp today.
A wandering saint told a dangerous snake: Stop biting people. And the snake listened, and became gentle.
But when the village boys saw it was harmless, they threw stones at it and swung it by the tail. When the saint came back, the snake was half dead.
Why did you let them? asked the saint. You told me not to bite, said the snake. I told you not to bite, said the saint. I never told you not to hiss!
Osho taught: gentleness is not weakness. You can be kind, and still say no. Where do you need to hiss a little today?
All the birds of the world set out together to find their king, the great Simorgh, who lived beyond seven valleys.
The way was terrible. Deserts, storms, endless doubts. One by one, the birds turned back, or fell. At last, only thirty were left.
Exhausted, the thirty birds came to the throne of the Simorgh. And when they looked, they saw only themselves, reflected in a lake.
In their language, Simorgh means thirty birds. Osho taught: what you search for is your own being. Look in the mirror today, kindly.
A rich farmer saw the Buddha begging for food and said: I plough and I sow, and then I eat. You should plough and sow too.
I do plough and sow, said the Buddha. Faith is my seed. Awareness is my plough. Patience is my ox. And the harvest is freedom from sorrow.
The farmer was quiet for a long time. Then he filled the Buddha's bowl with rice, and sat down beside him.
Osho taught: watch what you plant in your mind. Every day you are sowing something. What seed will you sow today?
